For claim c1:
Reuters reported on July 14, 2021, that a video claiming to show microchips in Pfizer-BioNTech COVID-19 vaccines was false, explaining that the video actually depicted research-level microrobots that cannot be added to vaccines. [1] The article further states that Marc Miskin, an assistant professor at the University of Pennsylvania and an author of the research on microrobots, confirmed that the claim of microrobots being added to vaccines is "a total fabrication" and that these robots are useless outside of a lab. [1]

The CDC states that COVID-19 vaccines do not contain microchips and are not administered to track movement, but rather to stimulate the immune system to produce antibodies against the disease. [2] Similarly, the Mayo Clinic also confirms that COVID-19 vaccines do not contain microchips and are made only with ingredients that help the body recognize and clear out the virus. [3] [4] Pfizer's official website also explicitly states that there are no microchips or tracking devices in any Pfizer vaccine, including the COVID-19 vaccine. [5]

The Indonesian Ministry of Communication and Information (Kominfo) has also debunked the claim, stating that the barcode on vaccine products is for tracking distribution, not for tracking vaccinated individuals. [6] [7] They clarified that videos circulating to support this claim were edited to create misleading statements. [6] The Indonesian Ministry of Health (Kemenkes) also issued a statement on May 28, 2021, calling the narrative that COVID-19 vaccines contain magnetic microchips untrue and urged the public not to be influenced by it. [8]

FactCheck.org explained on May 26, 2022, that ingredient lists for COVID-19 vaccines are publicly available and do not include microchips. [9] They also noted that claims about microchips in vaccines have circulated since the beginning of the pandemic, often misrepresenting statements from figures like Bill Gates or Pfizer's CEO. [10] [9] [11]
